stem: A wildlife biologist tags 83 birds at a nature reserve: 29 are finches, 37 are warblers, and 17 are thrushes. If one bird is selected at random from the tagged group, what is the probability that it is a warbler?
explanation: The probability of selecting a warbler is the number of warblers divided by the total number of birds: $\frac{37}{83}$. The value $\frac{29}{83}$ results from selecting the finch count instead of the warbler count. The value $\frac{17}{83}$ results from selecting the thrush count. The value $\frac{37}{46}$ results from dividing warblers by the sum of the other two groups ($29 + 17 = 46$) rather than the total, a fundamental misunderstanding of the probability formula.

stem: A survey of 200 employees at a technology firm asked whether they commute by car or by train and whether they work in engineering or in sales. Of the 200 employees, 118 commute by car and 82 commute by train. Among those who commute by car, 71 work in engineering. Among those who commute by train, 53 work in sales. Given that a randomly selected employee works in sales, what is the probability that this employee commutes by train?
explanation: First, determine the total number of sales employees. Car commuters in engineering: 71, so car commuters in sales: $118 - 71 = 47$. Train commuters in sales: 53, so train commuters in engineering: $82 - 53 = 29$. Total sales employees: $47 + 53 = 100$. The conditional probability that a sales employee commutes by train is $\frac{53}{100}$. The value $\frac{53}{82}$ divides by the total train commuters rather than the total sales employees, confusing P(train | sales) with P(sales | train). The value $\frac{53}{200}$ divides by the grand total instead of conditioning on sales. The value $\frac{82}{200}$ gives the unconditional probability of commuting by train, ignoring the sales condition entirely.

stem: A quality-control lab tests circuit boards from two production lines. Line P produces $61\%$ of all boards and has a defect rate of $4\%$. Line Q produces the remaining $39\%$ and has a defect rate of $7\%$. A board is selected at random from the combined output and is found to be defective. What is the probability, to the nearest thousandth, that it came from Line Q?
explanation: Using Bayes' theorem: $P(\text{defective}) = (0.61)(0.04) + (0.39)(0.07) = 0.0244 + 0.0273 = 0.0517$. Then $P(Q \mid \text{defective}) = \frac{(0.39)(0.07)}{0.0517} = \frac{0.0273}{0.0517} \approx 0.528$. The value $0.472$ is the complement, which results from computing $P(P \mid \text{defective})$ instead of $P(Q \mid \text{defective})$, effectively swapping the two lines. The value $0.273$ results from dividing $0.0273$ by $0.10$ (incorrectly adding the two defect rates $0.04 + 0.07 = 0.11$ rounded or miscomputed as $0.10$) instead of computing the weighted total probability correctly. The value $0.070$ simply states Line Q's defect rate, ignoring the Bayesian update entirely.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A random sample of 250 residents of a city found that $58\%$ favor expanding the public library. The margin of error for the survey is $\pm 4$ percentage points. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this result?

options.text: Exactly $58\%$ of all city residents favor expanding the library.
Between $54\%$ and $62\%$ of all city residents are likely to favor expanding the library.
Between $54\%$ and $62\%$ of the 250 residents surveyed favor expanding the library.
If the survey were repeated, exactly $58\%$ would favor expanding the library each time.

explanation: The margin of error defines a confidence interval around the sample proportion that is used to estimate the population parameter. Adding and subtracting 4 percentage points from $58\%$ gives the interval $54\%$ to $62\%$, which is the plausible range for the true proportion of all city residents who favor expanding the library. Stating that exactly $58\%$ of all residents favor it treats the sample statistic as the exact population parameter, ignoring sampling variability. Applying the interval to the 250 sampled residents confuses the population inference with the sample itself — the sample proportion is already known exactly. Claiming the result would be exactly $58\%$ every time misunderstands sampling variability; repeated samples yield different proportions.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: A researcher surveys a random sample of 400 college students at a large university and finds that 172 of them study more than 15 hours per week. The $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all students at the university who study more than 15 hours per week is $(0.39, 0.47)$. Which of the following statements is supported by this interval?

options.text: At most $39\%$ of all students at the university study more than 15 hours per week.
Exactly $43\%$ of all students at the university study more than 15 hours per week.
It is plausible that $45\%$ of all students at the university study more than 15 hours per week.
If the study were repeated with a sample of 100 students, the confidence interval would remain $(0.39, 0.47)$.

explanation: The $95\%$ confidence interval $(0.39, 0.47)$ means that all values within this interval are plausible values for the true population proportion. Since $0.45$ falls within $(0.39, 0.47)$, it is plausible that $45\%$ of all students study more than 15 hours per week. Claiming at most $39\%$ treats the lower bound as an upper limit, which reverses the meaning of the interval. Stating exactly $43\%$ (the sample proportion $172/400 = 0.43$) treats the point estimate as the exact population parameter, ignoring the uncertainty captured by the interval. Claiming the interval would remain the same with a sample of 100 students ignores that a smaller sample produces a wider margin of error, so the interval would change.

skill: Inference from Sample Statistics and Margin of Error
stem: Two independent random samples are drawn from the same population of registered voters. Sample 1 has 600 voters and produces a $95\%$ confidence interval of $(0.51, 0.59)$ for the proportion supporting a ballot measure. Sample 2 has 150 voters and produces a $95\%$ confidence interval of $(0.44, 0.64)$. Which of the following best explains the difference between the two intervals?

options.text: Sample 2 has a larger margin of error because its sample size is smaller, which increases variability in the sample proportion.
Sample 2's interval is wider because it was drawn from a different population than Sample 1.
Sample 1's interval is narrower because it has a higher confidence level than Sample 2.
The intervals differ because the two samples measured different proportions, proving the population proportion changed between surveys.

explanation: The margin of error is inversely related to the square root of the sample size. Sample 1 ($n = 600$) has a margin of error of about $0.04$, while Sample 2 ($n = 150$) has a margin of error of about $0.10$. The smaller sample produces more variability in the sample proportion, leading to a wider confidence interval. The claim that the samples are from different populations contradicts the stated premise that both are drawn from the same population. The claim that Sample 1 has a higher confidence level is false — both intervals are stated to be $95\%$ confidence intervals. The claim that the population proportion changed between surveys is unsupported; different sample proportions are expected due to sampling variability and do not prove a change in the true parameter.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A health researcher observes that patients who walk at least 8,000 steps per day have lower rates of high blood pressure than patients who walk fewer than 3,000 steps per day. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: Walking at least 8,000 steps per day causes lower blood pressure.
There is an association between walking more steps per day and lower rates of high blood pressure.
Patients who walk fewer than 3,000 steps per day should be prescribed medication for high blood pressure.
The researcher's data proves that exercise is the primary factor in controlling blood pressure.

explanation: Because this is an observational study (patients were not randomly assigned to step-count groups), the researcher can identify an association but cannot establish causation. Confounding variables such as overall fitness, diet, or age may explain the difference. Concluding that walking causes lower blood pressure inappropriately draws a causal inference from an observational design. Recommending medication goes beyond what the data support and introduces a treatment conclusion that the study did not test. Claiming the data proves exercise is the primary factor overstates the finding — observational data cannot prove a causal mechanism, and other factors were not controlled.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A university researcher wants to test whether a new note-taking method improves exam scores. She recruits 120 volunteers and randomly assigns 60 to use the new method and 60 to use their usual method for an entire semester. At the end of the semester, the group using the new method scores an average of 6 points higher on the final exam. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.text: The new note-taking method is likely to cause higher exam scores for all university students.
The new note-taking method likely caused the higher average exam score among the volunteers in this study.
There is an association between the new note-taking method and higher exam scores, but causation cannot be established.
The 6-point difference is too small to draw any conclusion from the study.

explanation: Because participants were randomly assigned to treatment and control groups, this is a randomized experiment, which does support a causal conclusion. However, because the participants are volunteers rather than a random sample of all university students, the result can be generalized only to the volunteers in the study, not to all university students. Generalizing to all university students oversteps the scope since the sample was self-selected volunteers. Claiming causation cannot be established applies to observational studies, not to randomized experiments where random assignment controls for confounding variables. Dismissing the 6-point difference as too small to draw any conclusion ignores the experimental design; the magnitude of a meaningful difference depends on statistical significance, not an arbitrary threshold.

skill: Evaluating Statistical Claims: Observational Studies and Experiments
stem: A pharmaceutical company conducts a study in which 300 patients with chronic migraines at a single hospital are randomly assigned to receive either a new drug or a placebo. After 12 weeks, the group receiving the new drug reports $41\%$ fewer migraine days on average than the placebo group. A medical journal reports: "The new drug has been proven to reduce migraines by $41\%$ in the general population." Which of the following best identifies the flaw in the journal's claim?

options.text: The study cannot establish causation because patients were not randomly assigned to groups.
The result can support a causal claim for the study participants, but generalizing to the entire general population is not justified because the sample was drawn from a single hospital.
The $41\%$ reduction is not statistically meaningful because the study lasted only 12 weeks.
The placebo group invalidates the study because placebos have no medical purpose.

explanation: The study uses random assignment, so a causal conclusion is supported for the study's participants. However, because all 300 patients were drawn from a single hospital rather than randomly sampled from the general population, the result cannot be generalized beyond patients similar to those at that hospital. The journal's claim that the drug is "proven" to work in the general population overstates the study's external validity. Claiming the study cannot establish causation is incorrect because patients were randomly assigned to treatment and placebo groups, which is stated in the stem. Dismissing the result because the study lasted only 12 weeks applies an arbitrary duration threshold rather than evaluating the study's design; a 12-week randomized trial can produce valid causal results. Claiming the placebo group invalidates the study misunderstands experimental design — placebos serve as the control condition necessary to isolate the effect of the drug.
